nameStory: The bedstraw hawkmoth gets its name from its caterpillars' favorite food: bedstraw plants (Galium species), which were once dried and used as mattress stuffing. The 'hawkmoth' part comes from their incredible flying abilities - these moths can hover like tiny hummingbirds and dart around with the agility of a hawk hunting its prey.
description: The bedstraw hawkmoth is a medium-sized sphinx moth with a robust, streamlined body built for powerful flight. Adults have a wingspan of about 2-3 inches and sport olive-green to brownish forewings with intricate darker markings that help them blend into bark and foliage. Their hindwings flash bright pink or rose-colored bands when they fly, creating a startling contrast. Like other sphinx moths, they're often mistaken for small hummingbirds as they hover at flowers to feed on nectar.

idTips.label: Pink hindwings
idTips.description: The most striking feature - bright pink or rose-colored bands on the hindwings that flash dramatically when the moth flies, but are hidden when at rest

idTips.label: Olive-brown forewings
idTips.description: Mottled olive-green to brown forewings with darker zigzag lines and pale spots that feel smooth to the touch, creating excellent camouflage against tree bark

idTips.label: Thick, fuzzy body
idTips.description: Robust, torpedo-shaped body covered in dense, soft scales that give it a velvety texture - much thicker and more substantial than typical moths

idTips.label: Hovering flight
idTips.description: Hovers at flowers like a hummingbird with rapid wingbeats that create a low humming sound, often feeding during twilight hours

idTips.label: Long proboscis
idTips.description: Extended tongue-like feeding tube that uncoils to reach deep into flowers - you might see it probing tube-shaped blooms while hovering

habitat: Look for bedstraw hawkmoths in open areas with abundant wildflowers, including meadows, gardens, roadsides, and forest edges throughout New England. They're particularly drawn to areas where bedstraw plants grow wild, such as grassy slopes and disturbed soils. Adults are most commonly spotted around nectar-rich flowers like honeysuckle, petunias, and four o'clocks during dusk and dawn.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring, with early individuals appearing in May. Look for them at dusk visiting early-blooming flowers like lilacs and wild cherry blossoms.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity occurs through summer months when adults are most abundant and actively feeding at flowers during twilight hours. This is the best time to spot their distinctive pink hindwings in flight.
seasonality.fall: Second-generation adults may appear in early fall, though they're less common. Caterpillars are actively feeding on bedstraw plants, preparing to pupate before winter.
seasonality.winter: Adults are absent - they overwinter as pupae buried in the soil. No above-ground activity to observe during cold months.

funFact: Bedstraw hawkmoths are incredible long-distance migrants that can fly hundreds of miles, and their caterpillars can actually change color from green to brown or even reddish depending on what they're eating and their surroundings - like tiny chameleons of the moth world!
confusionNotes: Often mistaken for hummingbirds due to their hovering behavior and size, but moths have feathery antennae instead of bills and are active at dusk rather than during bright daylight. Memory trick: if it's visiting flowers at twilight and you see a flash of pink, it's definitely the bedstraw hawkmoth, not a bird!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'hawkmoths,' these insects are completely harmless plant-eaters and pollinators - they get their name purely from their swift, agile flight patterns. The scientific name 'gallii' refers to the Galium genus of bedstraw plants, their host plants.
compareHints: Since this is the only Hyles species commonly found in New England, compare it to other sphinx moths in the region. Unlike the more common white-lined sphinx, the bedstraw hawkmoth lacks white stripes on the body and has distinctive pink (not orange or yellow) hindwing markings. It's also smaller and more subtly colored than the large five-spotted hawkmoth, which has yellow hindwings with black bands.
